title: Central Bank Admits Inflation Miss, Raises 2026 Forecast to 28%; Ankara Details Mecca Pact Military Mechanisms
subhead: Turkey's central bank lifted its end-2026 inflation forecast to 28% in a rare admission of a 'partial failure,' while Ankara unveiled concrete political and military mechanisms under the Saudi-Pakistan-Turkey defence pact.

sections.heading: Central Bank Raises 2026 Inflation Forecast to 28%, Concedes Miss
sections.body: Turkey's central bank lifted its end-2026 inflation forecast to 28% from 26% in its quarterly inflation report on August 13, while leaving its interim target for the period unchanged at 24%, Governor Fatih Karahan said. According to Bloomberg, the move brought the official forecast closer to market expectations and included a rare instance of self-criticism — an admission of a 'partial failure' on inflation. Anadolu-affiliated ilkha and Daily Sabah attribute the upgrade to higher energy, food and import costs and continued uncertainty from geopolitical developments, while the bank reiterated a vow to maintain a tight monetary stance.
sections.whyItMatters: The forecast revision signals the central bank now concedes it will miss its disinflation path, driven partly by the energy-cost shock from the Hormuz/Red Sea disruptions — pressure that complicates any easing and keeps the lira's stability tied to geopolitical risk.

sections.heading: Ankara Details Mecca Pact Mechanisms: Joint Exercises, Defence-Industry Cooperation
sections.body: Turkey's defence ministry laid out on Thursday (August 13) how the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement signed August 7 with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan will function, according to Al Jazeera and Reuters. The pact — which treats an armed attack on one member as an attack on all, akin to NATO's Article 5 — will see senior ministers and chiefs of staff grouped in strategic political and military mechanisms, with coordination at the highest level. The ministry said joint land, naval and air exercises, plus air-defence and unmanned-systems drills are planned, and that defence-industry cooperation would go beyond product supply toward joint development, production, technology transfer and sustainable maintenance. Unmanned and autonomous systems, electronic warfare and artificial intelligence capabilities are to be prioritised. Ankara reiterated the pact is not aimed at Iran, is open to expansion (with Egypt cited as a potential candidate), and does not replace existing alliances.
sections.whyItMatters: This turns a political declaration into an operational framework, giving the 'Islamic NATO' label practical content — and positioning Turkish defence industry (drones, EW, AI) as the technological backbone of a Sunni security bloc at a moment of US disengagement from the region.

sections.heading: Turkey Joins Jeddah Talks on Red Sea Shipping Coalition
sections.body: The Turkish defence ministry confirmed Ankara is participating in meetings in Jeddah aimed at establishing an international coalition to protect Red Sea shipping, Al Jazeera reported. The move comes as Houthi attacks on Saudi oil installations and Red Sea traffic have slowed shipping through Bab el-Mandeb, and as the Mecca pact partners coordinate on maritime security. Ministry spokesperson Rear Admiral Zeki Akturk framed regional instability around Israel, saying lasting peace requires an end to Israeli occupation and attacks in Gaza and Lebanon, and criticised Israel's rejection of the US-proposed 15-point Gaza Plan as evidence of 'regional expansionism.'
sections.whyItMatters: By joining the Jeddah coalition while building its own defence pact, Ankara is threading between Washington-led maritime security efforts and its own regional bloc — extending Turkish influence over the shipping lanes that carry much of its energy imports.

sections.heading: PKK Peace Law: Implementation Questions Remain
sections.body: Days after parliament passed the 12-article law establishing a legal framework for the PKK's disbandment, attention has turned to implementation, with Kurdistan24 reporting open questions over the fate of imprisoned PKK leaders and Abdullah Ocalan. The law, passed on August 10 per Reuters, marks a landmark step toward ending a decades-long conflict, but the mechanics of disarmament and reintegration remain unspecified.
sections.whyItMatters: The legal scaffolding is in place, but the test is whether the process survives its most delicate phase — what happens to senior PKK figures — without derailing the broader normalisation with Iraq and the Kurdish region.

sections.heading: Iraq-Kirkuk Oil Deal: Corridor Opening Follows Historic Accord
sections.body: The historic Ankara-Baghdad oil transport agreement that saw Turkish Petroleum (TPAO) take a stake in Kirkuk — signed earlier this week — sets up the reopening of the Ceyhan corridor as a major export route. No new developments emerged on Thursday beyond the deal's operational planning, with the focus now on restarting flows and how the arrangement interacts with the broader Kirkuk-Ceyhan pipeline economics that were suspended for years.
sections.whyItMatters: If flows ramp up, Turkey cements its position as the primary energy export corridor for Iraqi crude — a commercial anchor for the broader security and political cooperation with Baghdad signed alongside the accord.

bottomLine: Thursday's concrete news was economic and institutional: the central bank conceded it will miss its disinflation path, raising the 2026 forecast to 28% on energy and geopolitical shocks, while Ankara turned the Mecca defence pact from a declaration into a working framework of joint exercises, ministerial coordination and defence-industry integration. Together they point to a Turkey managing a tighter inflation bind at home while deepening its role as the military-technological core of a new Sunni security order — one it is simultaneously extending into Red Sea maritime security. The PKK peace law and Iraq oil corridor remain works in progress, with implementation the next test.
sources: Bloomberg, Daily Sabah, Anadolu/ilkha, Al Jazeera, Reuters, Kurdistan24, Middle East Eye, CFR, alhurra
